title: City of Regina plans to shut down public transit starting Monday
summary: ATU Canada president said workers have not had a new collective agreement for almost two years and the city chose to suspend services after the union said it would implement a ban on voluntary…

image.caption: A bus in Regina on a winter day (Bryan Eneas/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan

ATU Canada president said workers have not had a new collective agreement for almost two years and the city chose to suspend services after the union said it would implement a ban on voluntary overtime starting Monday.
Union leader says city chose this after the union announced overtime ban
There will be no public transit on Monday in Regina, according to the city.
The city's transit shutdown comes amid the ongoing collective bargaining agreement negotiations with the local transit workers' union, Amalgamated Transit Union (ATU) Local 588.

The city confirmed its director of transit operations sent employees a letter on Saturday advising them that only management and security personnel would be allowed to access Regina Transit facilities, yards and depots effective Monday at 3:00 a.m. CST.
A "formal lockout" will commence at 11:00 a.m. CST Monday.
The city says it cannot maintain a minimum level of service due to ATU Local 588 implementing an overtime ban starting Monday.
John Di Nino, president of ATU Canada, said the service suspension is the city's choice and the union does not want service to end.

"This is not something being initiated by the ATU. In fact this is the irresponsibility of city council who's allowing this to happen. They're penalizing their members because they can't come to the table and negotiate a fair contract for transit workers. "

He said workers have not had a new collective agreement for almost two years and he confirmed the city chose to suspend services after the union said it would implement a ban on voluntary overtime starting Monday.
John Di Nino, president of ATU Canada. (ATU Canada)
"The city is using a power play. They're suggesting that without the voluntary overtime that they cannot maintain their service levels, again that's a farce," he said.
"If an employer relies on overtime to fill shifts to provide a service, then they're not managing the property correctly. That only tells us that more workers are needed to maintain regular service."
He said workers will still report to work on Monday morning.

blocks.text: A statement the city provided to CBC said "The decision to impact transit service was not taken lightly. Resident safety is a top priority of the city, and as the weather continues to get colder the city needed to ensure transit service is reliable so that no one is left outside waiting for a ride."
Paratransit service will continue, according to the city's website.

blocks.text: "Transit employees are valued, both by the city and residents who rely on them every day. The agreement must balance staff needs with the interests of residents and taxpayers," according to the statement.
On Monday, Environment Canada projects the temperature of Regina to be –4 C during the day and –11 C at night.
According to De Nino and the city's letter to workers, they will not be paid after Monday morning while the suspension occurs.
The union has also raised other issues such as pay, benefits and safety while trying to negotiate the agreement, Di Nino said.
The city did not respond to CBC's additional requests for comment by time of publication.
